table.title: [val2] SLA tiers
table.md:
| Tier | Monthly uptime commitment | Service credit | Support channels |
|---|--:|--:|---|
| Standard | 99.5% | 10% | Email, community forum |
| Professional | 99.9% | 25% | Email, chat, phone during business hours in the customer's primary time zone |
| Mission-critical | 99.99% | 50% | 24/7 phone with a named technical account manager |

understanding.purpose: Compare SLA tiers by their uptime commitments, service credits, and available support channels.
understanding.reading: Readers scan the tier names down the first column, compare the uptime and credit figures across tiers, then read the support details for the tiers of interest.
groups: Monthly uptime commitment and service credit are paired quantitative terms for comparing each tier.
Tier identifies each row; support channels describe the service available with that tier.
keep_intact: Tier names and percentage values should remain readable as units.
Avoid splitting words in headers and support descriptions where practical.
may_wrap: The multiword column headers can wrap between words.
Support-channel descriptions can wrap naturally and establish row height that other cells can share.

preferred.name: r2B
preferred.note: Combine an intact tier label with r1B's more naturally wrapped support descriptions. This favors legibility and shorter rows at the cost of additional scrolling.

acceptable.name: r1B
acceptable.note: Try a modest reduction from r0C’s support width, seeking much of its compact row rhythm with less overflow.

acceptable.name: r2A
acceptable.note: Widen Tier enough to keep Mission-critical on one line, while retaining r1A's moderate support width and readable wrapping. This adds 21px of horizontal scrolling.

acceptable.name: r3A
acceptable.note: Use a support width between r2A and r2B to test whether better wrapping is possible with a smaller scrolling cost than r2B.

acceptable.name: r3B
acceptable.note: Give support descriptions more room to improve row rhythm, accepting additional horizontal scrolling while preserving the compact comparison columns.

acceptable.name: r3C
acceptable.note: Reduce the tier column to its longest unbreakable word width so more support text appears initially; test whether wrapping Mission-critical at its hyphen is an acceptable tradeoff.

bad.name: r1C
bad.note: Give support just enough width to keep its longest word intact, testing the smallest practical overflow while preserving readable tier names and headers.
bad.why: The narrow support column turns the longer descriptions into tall stacks of up to eight lines, leaving large areas of empty space in the other columns.

bad.name: r2C
bad.note: Keep tier names intact and test a middle ground between r1A and r1C for support width, reducing scrolling while allowing more wrapping than the balanced design.
bad.why: The support descriptions wrap into as many as seven lines, making the rows disproportionately tall and weakening comparisons across the table.

rationale: r2B keeps every tier name on one line and gives the long support descriptions enough room to read in coherent phrases. The uptime and credit columns remain compact and easy to compare vertically. Horizontal scrolling is substantial, but the first view includes all three identifying and numeric columns, while the support column begins at the right edge.

general: Give row identifiers enough room to remain recognizable while scanning across rows.
Judge a text-heavy column by the resulting row rhythm as well as by its width; excessive wrapping can leave neighboring cells visually stranded.
When horizontal scrolling is necessary, preserve a useful set of columns in the initial viewport.
specific: The support descriptions need much more width than the percentage values.
The 126px tier column keeps Mission-critical on one line; at 105px it wraps at the hyphen.
A 180px support column reduces wrapping substantially compared with 130px, at the cost of additional scrolling.

tradeoffs: r1B and r3C reduce scrolling by 21px but wrap Mission-critical. r3B makes the first data row shorter by widening support, at the cost of another 20px of horizontal scrolling.
uncertain: The width ranges are conservative estimates from the supplied renderings, not tested breakpoints. A designer may reasonably prefer r1B for its smaller scroll distance or r3B for its more compact rows.

critique.good: The whole table fits in the viewport, and the percentage values are easy to compare in aligned columns.
critique.problems: The header is unusually tall, Professional breaks inside the word, and the support descriptions form narrow vertical stacks. The resulting tall rows make it harder to connect each tier with its terms.
critique.cause: At 90px, the tier column leaves too little space for Professional. The 100px uptime and 70px credit columns force header words to split, while the 99px support column leaves little room for natural phrase wrapping.

critique.good: Tier names and the quantitative headers are more legible, and the table extends only a short distance beyond the viewport.
critique.problems: The support column is partly outside the initial view and still wraps into very long stacks. The large row heights make comparisons across tiers laborious.
critique.cause: The 105px tier, 112px uptime, and 75px credit columns protect their longest words, but the 98px support column remains too narrow for the descriptions.

critique.good: The wider support column lets descriptions wrap into readable phrases and makes the rows much more compact. Tier names and quantitative values remain easy to scan.
critique.problems: A substantial portion of the support column lies beyond the viewport, so readers must scroll to read the full descriptions. Its relatively short rows also make the three-line uptime header visually prominent.
critique.cause: The 200px support column creates a 133px overflow; the 112px uptime column wraps its header across three lines.

critique.good: The tier names and both quantitative columns remain visible at first sight, making the main comparisons easy. Support text wraps without mid-word splits, and the row heights leave the figures comfortably aligned with their tiers.
critique.problems: Mission-critical wraps at its hyphen, weakening the row label. Much of the support column lies beyond the viewport, while the long Professional description makes its row noticeably taller.
critique.cause: The 105px tier column provides only 84px of text space. The 150px support column creates a moderate horizontal overflow and wraps the longest description to five lines.

critique.good: The wider support column gives the longest description a more natural rhythm and reduces the Professional row height. The quantitative columns remain visible at first sight.
critique.problems: Mission-critical still wraps, and the wider table requires more horizontal scrolling to read support details. The extra width brings little benefit to the other rows.
critique.cause: The tier column remains 105px, while increasing support to 180px raises overflow to 113px.

critique.good: The smaller overflow makes more of the support column visible initially, and words remain intact.
critique.problems: Support descriptions become narrow stacks of short lines, making rows unusually tall and comparisons across tiers harder. The support header also wraps, and Mission-critical remains on two lines.
critique.cause: The 110px support column leaves only 89px for text, forcing the longest description to eight lines. The 105px tier column still cannot accommodate the full tier name on one line.

critique.good: Tier names and percentages stay intact, and the two quantitative columns are compact enough to compare easily. The support text wraps without splitting words.
critique.problems: The support descriptions create an uneven rhythm, especially in the much taller Professional row. Most of the support column lies beyond the initial viewport.
critique.cause: The 150px support column gives long descriptions only 129px of text width, while the first three columns already occupy 313px.

critique.good: The wider support column reduces the tallest cell from five lines to four and makes the table shorter and more balanced. Tier names, percentages and words remain intact.
critique.problems: The wider table requires more horizontal scrolling, and only a sliver of the support column appears initially. The quantitative headers remain relatively tall.
critique.cause: The 180px support column improves wrapping but increases overflow to 134px; the 112px uptime column wraps its header across three lines.

critique.good: It has the least horizontal overflow, and words and tier names remain intact.
critique.problems: The narrow support column produces very tall, uneven rows and leaves large areas of empty space in the other columns. The support header also wraps, while the descriptions remain largely outside the initial viewport.
critique.cause: At 130px, the support column provides only 109px of text width, forcing the longest description into seven lines.

review.method: two fresh-context blind reviews; letters shuffled; includes browser auto layout and equal widths as neutral references

r1C.why: The support text wraps into many short lines, making the middle row especially tall. The last tier name also wraps, while the support column extends beyond the viewport.

r2B.why: Tier names and percentages remain intact, and the support descriptions wrap into relatively few lines. The support column requires horizontal scrolling.

r2A.why: Tier names and numeric columns scan clearly, but the support descriptions wrap more than in B and still require horizontal scrolling.

ref_equal.why: Everything fits within the viewport, but words split in the uptime header, tier name and support text. The resulting tall rows are difficult to scan.

ref_auto.why: The narrow support column produces a tall, fragmented block of text, while the last tier name wraps. Some support text still lies beyond the viewport.

r1B.why: The support descriptions have room to wrap into relatively few lines, and the numeric columns are easy to compare. The last tier name wraps and the support column requires horizontal scrolling.

raw.unsure: The images do not show the full right edge of the scrolling layouts, so the total scroll distance and complete support-column wrapping are difficult to judge.

r1B.why: The numeric columns scan clearly, but Mission-critical wraps and much of the support column lies beyond the initial viewport.

r1C.why: The narrow support column creates very tall rows and leaves text extending beyond the viewport; Mission-critical also wraps.

ref_equal.why: The table fits the viewport, but commitment, Professional and community split within words. The support column is difficult to scan.

r2A.why: Tier names stay intact and the numeric columns are easy to compare. The support column requires horizontal scrolling.

r2B.why: Tier names and numeric values stay intact, and the support text appears to wrap less than in D. The support column still requires horizontal scrolling.

ref_auto.why: The support column is very narrow, producing tall rows and leaving some text beyond the viewport. Mission-critical also wraps.

raw.unsure: The supplied image display cuts off the right side of the wider layouts, so I cannot fully judge the support text or the total scrolling distance.

provenance.note: AI visual design judgement; not a human reading study
